Chapter Two: The Traits and Habits of Exceptional Forecasters
So, now that we’ve recognized just how tricky prediction can be, let’s dive into what actually sets superforecasters apart. You might expect these folks to be geniuses, or maybe to have access to some kind of hidden intel. But, honestly, that’s not it.
What makes superforecasters different isn’t some secret sauce—it’s the way they think, how they process information, and how they handle feedback. At the heart of it all, superforecasting is about a special attitude toward the world. It’s a mix of curiosity, humility, and some serious analytical chops.
Instead of sticking to one viewpoint no matter what, these people treat their beliefs like hypotheses—something to test, poke at, and maybe even toss out if the evidence changes. They’re perfectly okay with ambiguity, and they’ll change their minds if the facts point in a new direction.
Now, let’s break down the key traits and habits that really stand out in top forecasters.
First up, active open-mindedness. Superforecasters don’t just look for answers that confirm what they already believe. They’re actually searching for information that could prove them wrong. Instead of digging in their heels, they’re focused on uncovering the truth—even if that means admitting they made a mistake.
Second, there’s analytical thinking. These folks are pros at taking big, complicated problems and breaking them down into smaller, bite-sized pieces. Rather than making a sweeping prediction about some huge event, they’ll look at all the moving parts and figure out the odds for each one.
Next, we have probabilistic reasoning. Rather than making bold, black-and-white statements like “This is definitely going to happen,” superforecasters talk in probabilities: 30%, 60%, 90%. They’re comfortable with uncertainty, and they know how to express it.
Another important habit is frequent updating. As new information pops up, superforecasters are quick to update their predictions. For them, forecasting isn’t a one-and-done kind of deal—it’s an ongoing process.
And finally, there’s a genuine willingness to learn from feedback. They pay close attention to how their past predictions turned out. When they get something wrong, they don’t get defensive—they look for ways to do better next time.
Let’s make this more concrete. Imagine a team is asked to predict if a country’s leader will be replaced in the next year. Most people might just go with their gut or look at general trends. But a superforecaster? They’ll dig into recent political developments, public sentiment, and even past leadership changes. They’ll break the big question into smaller ones—like, is there a history of sudden changes? Are there signs of unrest? How’s the current leader’s health?
Then, they’ll assign probabilities to each factor, combine those estimates, and come up with an overall likelihood. And as new headlines roll in, they’ll adjust their prediction, staying flexible.
The goal isn’t to be right every single time. It’s about being less wrong, more often. Superforecasters get that the future is uncertain, but they work to shrink that uncertainty and update their views as new things happen.
Here’s a super helpful image: think about a weather forecaster. Instead of declaring, “It’ll rain tomorrow,” a skilled forecaster says, “There’s a 70% chance of rain.” That kind of statement captures both their judgment and the natural uncertainty. And if, over time, it really does rain about 70% of the time when they say it will, you know they’re well-calibrated.
Superforecasters use this approach everywhere—from geopolitics to business decisions, and even everyday choices. Their results aren’t about luck. It’s all about disciplined thinking and a real openness to learning.
